{{Short description|American physicist}}
'''Bernard J. Eastlund''' (1938 – December 12, 2007) was an American [[physicist]] who received his [[Bachelor of Science|B.S.]] in physics from [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]] (MIT) and his [[Doctor of Philosophy|Ph.D.]] in physics from [[Columbia University]]. In 1970 he received a Special Achievement Certificate from the [[United States Atomic Energy Commission|U. S. Atomic Energy Commission]] for co-invention of the "[[fusion torch]]."<ref name="FPN">{{cite web|title=In Memoriam: Bernard J. Eastlund|url=https://aries.pppl.gov/FPA/ARC07/fpn07-70.shtml|website=Fusion Power Associates|publisher=US Department of Energy Office of Fusion Energy Sciences|accessdate=26 May 2017}}</ref>

== Career ==
Eastlund attended MIT, receiving a B.S Physics degree in 1960. In 1965, he received a Ph.D. in plasma physics from Columbia University, and spent 3 years as a post-doc fellow there. Eastlund became a staff member at the fusion office at the U.S. Atomic Energy Commission (USAEC) in 1968. The USAEC recognized Eastlund's paper, "The Fusion Torch" co-authored with William C. Gough, with a Special Award in 1970. [[Scientific American]] magazine published a review of fusion programs by Eastland and Gough in 1971.<ref name="FPN" />

In 1974, Eastlund left the USAEC and co-founded Fusion Systems Corporation, which focused on ultraviolet-based curing technology with applications in the packaging and manufacturing industry. Fusion Systems technology was used for fast-drying industrial requirements such as labels on Coors beer cans and furniture varnishes. The company sold in 1997 for $193 million.<ref name="FPN" />

In 1979, Eastlund left Fusion Systems to become vice president of energy research for BDM Corporation. Eastlund served as a member of the board of directors and also as treasurer at Fusion Power Associates. After leaving BDM, Eastlund worked for Atlantic Richfield Corporation. In 1987 he founded Production Technologies International Corporation and in 1996 he founded Eastlund Scientific Enterprises Corporation. In 2003, Eastlund was awarded a U.S. House of Representatives Certificate of Recognition for contributions to homeland security technology.<ref name="FPN" />

Eastlund was in favor of funding research into [[weather modification]] and control that could reduce the impact of severe weather. He envisioned "concepts for electromagnetic wave interactions with the atmosphere that, among a range of jobs, could be applied to weather modification research" and that such research could mature to a new science in 10 or 20 years.<ref name="USA">{{cite web|last1=David|first1=Leonard|title=Science and Space|url=https://usatoday30.usatoday.com/tech/science/discoveries/2005-10-31-military-weather_x.htm|website=USA Today|publisher=USA Today|accessdate=26 May 2017}}</ref>

He was active in [[astrophysics]], and later work included co-authoring papers regarding [[pulsar]]s and [[Gamma-ray burst|gamma bursters]] presented in the [[The Astrophysical Journal|Astrophysical Journal]] and at scientific symposiums.<ref>Böttcher, M., Eastlund, B., & Miller, B. 1997, in Fourth Huntsville Gamma-Ray Burst Symp., ed. C. A. Meegan, R. D. Preece, & T. M. Koshut (New York: AIP)</ref><ref name="Nature">{{cite journal|last1=Eastlund|first1=Bernard J.|title=Low Mode Coherent Synchrotron Radiation and Pulsar Phenomena|journal=Nature|date=January 31, 1970|volume=225|page=430|bibcode = 1970Natur.225..430E |doi = 10.1038/225430a0|issue=5231|s2cid=4264829}}</ref><ref name="AAS">{{cite web|title=Rice University Department of Space Physics and Astronomy – 4.2.6 High Energy Astrophysics|url=https://aas.org/archives/BAAS/v31n1/bas_issue1-31_047901bas.pdf|website=AAS.org|publisher=[[American Astronomical Society]]|accessdate=26 May 2017}}</ref><ref name="AJ">{{cite journal|last1=Eastlund|first1=B.J.|last2=Miller|first2=B.|last3=Michel|first3=F. Curtis|title=Emission from Closed and Filled Magnetospheric Shells and Its Application to the Crab Pulsar|journal=The Astrophysical Journal|date=1997|volume=483|issue=2|doi=10.1086/304292|bibcode=1997ApJ...483..857E|pages=857–867|doi-access=free}}</ref>

In later years, he continued to collaborate with Gough and George Miley on their fusion torch concepts. Eastlund died December 12, 2007, at his home in St. Louis, survived by his wife, Sherrie, and several children.<ref name="FPN" />

== Patents ==
Eastlund authored 53 peer reviewed scientific papers and 23 US patents for applications such as well-drilling, sterilization of medical devices, high intensity lighting, and atmospheric plasma heating.<ref name="FT">{{cite web|last1=Taylor|first1=Keith|title=Team – Bernard J. Eastlund|url=http://www.fusiontorch.com/Team.html|website=Fusion Torch|publisher=Fusiontorch.com|accessdate=26 May 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170425030053/http://www.fusiontorch.com/Team.html|archive-date=25 April 2017|url-status=dead}}</ref><ref name="Justia">{{cite web|title=Patents by Inventor Bernard J. Eastlund|url=http://patents.justia.com/inventor/bernard-j-eastlund|website=JUSTIA Patents|publisher=Justia.com|accessdate=26 May 2017}}</ref>

One of Eastlund's patents (US4686605 A) described an adaptation of concepts first proposed by [[Nikola Tesla]]. Eastlund's ''"Method and apparatus for altering a region in the earth's atmosphere, ionosphere, and/or [[magnetosphere]]"'', described as "grandiose", proposed a 40-mile square radio transmitter that used Alaskan natural gas to generate current to create [[electromagnetic radiation]] that would excite a section of the [[ionosphere]]. Eastlund's patent speculated on "possible ramifications and potential future developments" including [[Magnetotellurics|magnetotelluric]] surveys, local weather modification, and missile defense.<ref name="Patent">{{cite web|last1=Eastlund|first1=Bernard J.|title=Method and apparatus for altering a region in the earth's atmosphere, ionosphere, and/or magnetosphere|url=https://patents.google.com/patent/US4686605|website=IFI CLAIMS Patent Services|publisher=Google Patents|access-date=29 May 2017}}</ref><ref name="Farmer1995"/><ref name="Dunning">{{Skeptoid|id=4122|number=122|title=HAARP Myths|accessdate=26 May 2017}}</ref><ref name="Naiditch">{{cite web|last1=Naiditch|first1=David|title=Is Baked Alaska Half-Baked?|url=https://www.skeptic.com/eskeptic/10-03-03/|website=Skeptic Magazine|publisher=The Skeptics Society|accessdate=26 May 2017}}</ref> Eastlund later claimed that [[HAARP]] was built using his patents, prompting [[Conspiracy theory|conspiracy theorists]] such as [[Nick Begich III|Nick Begich]] to claim that HAARP is capable of secretly controlling the weather.<ref name="Popsci">{{cite web|last1=Street|first1=Abe|title=The Military's Mystery Machine|url=https://www.popsci.com/military-aviation-space/article/2008-06/militarys-mystery-machine#page-3|website=Popular Science|accessdate=26 May 2017}}</ref><ref>Zey, Michael G. ''The Future Factor: Forces Transforming Human Destiny'' Transaction Publishers; New edition (30 April 2004) {{ISBN|978-0-7658-0591-1}} p. 39</ref> According to HAARP program manager John L. Heckscher, "HAARP certainly does not have anything to do with Eastlund's thing, that is just crazy. What we have here is a premier scientific research facility with military applications."<ref name="Farmer1995">Mark Farmer. ''[https://books.google.com/books?id=nSeBEQ2wGlUC&pg=PA79 Popular Science]''. September 1995 ed. Bonnier Corporation; September 1995. [[International Standard Serial Number|ISSN]]&nbsp;[//www.worldcat.org/search?fq=x0:jrnl&q=n2:01617370 01617370]. pp. 79–.</ref>
